content:
Apple TV has just secured global streaming rights to Australian crime series 《Dustfall》, marking the second time this streaming platform has deviated from its strategy of only showing its own original content.

Apple is beginning to introduce more licensed television series, deviating from its all-original-content strategy.

Since its launch in 2019, Apple TV has consistently rejected the traditional streaming platform approach of relying on licensed content, instead focusing on original productions.

Apple has been very consistent in its strategy of only showing its own original content. Until recently, the only exceptions have been children's programming that complements its original content (such as Peanuts holiday specials), as well as limited-run affiliated films.

However, that changed this week, with the highly acclaimed comedy 《Small Prophets》 officially premiering — this hit British series was acquired by Apple this past summer.

《Small Prophets》 looks like a smart acquisition. Early reviews have praised it as a 'masterpiece', and possibly 'the best series Apple has on offer this year'.

Today, Apple announced its second acquisition. The Australian crime drama 《Dustfall》, starring Anna Torv, will join the streaming platform in 2027.

Like 《Small Prophets》, 《Dustfall》 is produced by an international production company, having aired in some overseas markets before its global debut on Apple TV.

It's clear that Apple's approach to acquiring content is now different from before.

Although the platform has not abandoned its successful original-focused approach, bringing in quality series from around the world to enrich its library does represent a significant strategic shift.

I'm very interested to keep an eye on whether this trend will accelerate going forward.

What are your thoughts on Apple TV bringing in third-party series? Feel free to share with us in the comments section.

Apple TV costs US$14.99 per month, with discounts available through the Apple One bundle.
